book.title: Scrum: The Art of Doing Twice the Work in Half the Time
book.author: Jeff Sutherland and J.J. Sutherland

confidence_note: Origin facts from Wikipedia pages on Scrum and Jeff Sutherland, book not read. Old text's brain-research and sector claims dropped. Facts are about the history, not the book's own scenes, so attribution to the book is kept light.
facts: In 1986 Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka published 'The New New Product Development Game' in Harvard Business Review, based on case studies of firms in the car, photocopier and printer industries.
They called it a rugby approach: one cross-functional team that tries to go the distance as a unit, passing the ball back and forth.
In the early 1990s Jeff Sutherland, John Scumniotales and Jeff McKenna built a similar approach at Easel Corporation and called it scrum.
Sutherland had flown RF-4C Phantom reconnaissance missions from Udorn in Thailand, including missions in the Vietnam War.
Sutherland and Ken Schwaber merged their ideas and presented a paper at OOPSLA '95.
A sprint is normally one week to one month, most often two weeks.
A summary of the book says the FBI's Virtual Case File project spent about $170 million over five years with nothing usable.
scene_details: a rugby team passing the ball
tension: A software method got its name from a rugby formation used in a 1986 paper about cars and copiers.
opening_idea: Open on the rugby scrum in a paper about photocopiers.

lessons.idea: Move the whole team through the work together instead of passing it down a line
lessons.anchor: rugby 'passing the ball back and forth'; Everyday: a kitchen crew where one person writes the menu, another buys, a third cooks, versus all three planning together each morning

reflect_final: Where does work in your team pass from one person to the next, and what would change if they worked on it together?

use_cases.situation: A project is handed from design to build to testing
use_cases.move: Takeuchi and Nonaka described a team passing the ball back and forth, like rugby. Can design and testing sit together for the first week?

use_cases.situation: Siblings split the chores, each doing their part alone
use_cases.move: Let's do the kitchen together for ten minutes and see who needs what.

use_cases.situation: You plan a long task alone, step by step
use_cases.move: I will do a two-week sprint, then see what I actually have.

pocket_idea: Scrum took its name from a rugby team passing the ball back and forth. Plan the work together, not in a line.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The word scrum came from a 1986 paper that compared product teams to rugby, long before it named a software method.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In 1986 two professors, Takeuchi and Nonaka, studied car, copier and printer firms and compared their teams to rugby, passing the ball back and forth. In the early 1990s Jeff Sutherland, a former reconnaissance pilot, used a similar approach at Easel and called it scrum. In 1995 he and Ken Schwaber presented it in a paper.
